name: Chasok Tangnam
when: Nov–Dec, full moon of Mangsir (Senchengla in the Limbu calendar)
summary: Chasok Tangnam is the Limbu harvest festival, held on the full moon of Mangsir, when the first grain of the year is offered to the goddess Yuma Sammang and other deities. In Soreng district, where about one person in seven speaks Limbu at home, it is celebrated in villages and community gatherings.
body: Wikipedia describes Chasok Tangnam as a festival of the Limbu people falling on the full moon of Senchengla, the Limbu name for the month of Mangsir in the Nepali calendar, usually in late November or December. Its heart is an offering of the first harvest to Yuma Sammang, the mother goddess of the Limbu, and to other deities, before the new grain is eaten, followed by visits between families and neighbours.

Soreng district has one of the strongest Limbu presences in Sikkim. The 2011 census found Limbu to be the first language of about 14 percent of people in what is now the district, second only to Nepali, and villages around Soreng and Daramdin are home to many Limbu families. Celebrations range from household rituals led by a Limbu priest to community programmes organised by local Limbu associations, with prayers, cultural performances and shared food.

Venues and programmes are set locally each year, and much of the festival happens in homes, not on a public stage. If you are staying in a Limbu homestay around Soreng or Daramdin in late November or December, ask your hosts whether they are marking Chasok Tangnam and whether guests may watch. Dates follow the lunar calendar, so check current status before you travel.
tips: Ask your homestay hosts before your trip whether Chasok Tangnam falls during your stay and whether guests may join.
Dress modestly, follow the lead of your hosts and ask before photographing rituals, priests or elders.
Late November and December are also orange season in Soreng, so combine the festival with a farm visit.

faqs.a: On the full moon of the Nepali month of Mangsir, called Senchengla in the Limbu calendar, which usually falls in late November or December. The exact date changes each year with the lunar calendar. Ask us or your homestay hosts for the confirmed date, and check current status before you travel.

The first harvest of the year is offered to Yuma Sammang, the Limbu mother goddess, and other deities, usually with prayers led by a Limbu priest, before the new grain is eaten. Families then visit each other and share food. Community programmes may add cultural performances and speeches.

faqs.q: Can tourists attend Chasok Tangnam in Soreng?
faqs.a: Visitors are often welcome at community programmes, and homestay guests may be invited to watch family rituals. It is a religious occasion, so ask first, follow your hosts' lead and accept if a ritual is private. Venues and timings are set locally each year.

faqs.q: Why is Soreng a good place to experience Limbu culture?
faqs.a: Soreng district has one of Sikkim's largest Limbu communities: about 14 percent of residents named Limbu as their first language in the 2011 census, second only to Nepali. Villages around Soreng and Daramdin have Limbu homestays where you can learn about food, festivals and the Mundhum oral tradition.

name: Tamu Lhosar at the Gurung Gumpa
when: Around 30 December, 15 Poush in the Nepali calendar
summary: Tamu Lhosar is the Gurung new year. Near Rinchenpong it is marked at Rinchen Choling Monastery, the Gurung Gumpa at Meghi Dara, which the Soreng district administration says observes it on 30 December, with Gurung food, dress and traditions on show.
body: Wikipedia describes Tamu Lhosar as the new year of the Gurung people, celebrated on the 15th of Poush in the Nepali calendar, which falls at the end of December. Like the Tibetan, Sherpa and Tamang new years, it follows a twelve-year cycle in which each year is represented by an animal, and Lhosar marks the passing of one animal year to the next. People wear traditional dress, and songs and dances such as the Ghatu are part of the celebrations.

Near Rinchenpong, the focus is Rinchen Choling Monastery at Meghi Dara, a short walk from Rinchenpong town. The Soreng district administration says it was established in 1996 by the Gurung Buddhist Society, which is why it is also called the Gurung Gumpa, and that it stands on the ruins of a meditation retreat once used by Reesum Lama. The district site says Tamu Lhosar is observed at the monastery on 30 December each year, with the Gurung community showing its culture, food and traditions.

For travellers in Rinchenpong over the Christmas and New Year week, this is a chance to see a community festival rather than a staged show. Programmes are organised by the community and may change, so ask at the monastery or your homestay a few days ahead, and check current status before you travel. Rinchenpong is busy that week, so book rooms early.
tips: Book Rinchenpong or Kaluk rooms well ahead for the last week of December, the busiest time of winter.
Ask at Rinchen Choling Monastery or your homestay a few days before 30 December for the programme.
Dress warmly: late December evenings on the Rinchenpong ridge fall to about 3–5 °C.

faqs.q: When is Tamu Lhosar celebrated near Rinchenpong?
faqs.a: The Soreng district administration says it is observed at Rinchen Choling Monastery, the Gurung Gumpa near Rinchenpong, on 30 December every year. That matches the 15th of Poush in the Nepali calendar, the date Wikipedia gives for Tamu Lhosar. Check current status before you travel, as programmes are set by the community.

faqs.q: Where is the Gurung Gumpa near Rinchenpong?
faqs.a: Rinchen Choling Monastery stands at Meghi Dara, a short walk from Rinchenpong town. The district site says the Gurung Buddhist Society established it in 1996, on the ruins of a meditation retreat once used by Reesum Lama. Ask at your homestay for the path.

The Gurung community welcomes the new animal year with prayers, traditional dress, songs, dances such as the Ghatu, and shared food. At the Gurung Gumpa near Rinchenpong, the district site says the community showcases its culture, food and traditions. The programme varies from year to year.

faqs.q: Can visitors join Tamu Lhosar celebrations?
faqs.a: Visitors are generally welcome to watch community celebrations respectfully. Dress modestly, follow the organisers' directions and ask before photographing people. It is a community festival, not a tourist event, so keep a low profile and enjoy the food stalls if there are any.

name: Drukpa Tshe-zi at Reesum Gumpa
when: Jul–Aug, 4th day of the 6th Tibetan month (lunar)
community: Buddhist (Bhutia, Lepcha, Sherpa, Gurung and others)
summary: Drukpa Tshe-zi marks the day the Buddha gave his first sermon at Sarnath. The Soreng district administration says people from around Rinchenpong climb to Reesum Gumpa, the old hilltop monastery above the village, to pray and offer freshly harvested fruit and vegetables.
body: Drukpa Tshe-zi falls on the 4th day of the 6th month of the Tibetan lunar calendar, usually in July or August. The Soreng district administration's festival page explains that it commemorates the Buddha's first sermon, the teaching of the Four Noble Truths to his five disciples at the deer park in Sarnath. It is one of the important Buddhist days in Sikkim, and a state holiday is usually declared for it.

Around Rinchenpong, the district site says, people visit Reesum Gumpa on this day to offer prayers and seek blessings, and bring freshly harvested fruits and vegetables as offerings. Reesum Gumpa stands in Upper Hathidhunga on the forested crest above Rinchenpong; the district describes it as one of the oldest monasteries in Sikkim, a wooden building with a stone wall around it. The forest walk up from Rinchenpong takes about 30–45 minutes each way.

Drukpa Tshe-zi falls in the monsoon, so expect rain, mud and leeches on the trail, and cloud over the mountains. It is a quiet, local observance rather than a festival with dances. If you are in Rinchenpong that day, walk up early, dress modestly, and leave a small offering. Dates follow the lunar calendar, so check current status before you travel.
tips: Wear shoes with grip and carry a rain jacket and leech socks for the monsoon walk to Reesum Gumpa.
Bring a small offering of fruit if you wish, following local custom on the day.
Ask your homestay the evening before what time people usually walk up.

faqs.a: A Buddhist observance on the 4th day of the 6th Tibetan month, usually July or August, marking the Buddha's first sermon on the Four Noble Truths at Sarnath, as the Soreng district site explains. In Sikkim people visit monasteries to pray, and near Rinchenpong many climb to Reesum Gumpa with offerings.

It follows the Tibetan lunar calendar, falling on the 4th day of the 6th month, which is usually in late July or August. The Sikkim government's holiday list gives the date each year. Check current status before you travel, or ask us for the confirmed date.

faqs.q: How do I reach Reesum Gumpa from Rinchenpong?
faqs.a: Walk up the forest trail from Rinchenpong towards Upper Hathidhunga, about 30–45 minutes each way through oak and rhododendron. Ask your homestay for the start of the path. In the monsoon the trail is muddy and leeches are common, so wear good shoes and carry a rain jacket.

faqs.q: Is Drukpa Tshe-zi a good time to visit Rinchenpong?
faqs.a: Only if you do not mind rain. It falls in the monsoon, when cloud usually hides Kangchenjunga and roads can be slowed by slides. In return, Rinchenpong is quiet, green and cheaper. For mountain views, October to April is far better.
